did_you_know.text: Did you know? The statue Nebuchadnezzar erected was made of gold. It was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, and it was set up in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.
Did you know? Nebuchadnezzar summoned a wide range of officials from throughout the kingdom to the statue’s dedication ceremony, including satraps, prefects, governors, and provincial rulers.
Did you know? The royal decree required everyone to bow down to the statue as soon as they heard music played on the horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp, pipes, and other instruments.
Did you know? Anyone who refused to bow down to the statue was to be thrown immediately into a blazing furnace.
Did you know? The Chaldeans accused the Jews before the king, thereby beginning the confrontation over the faithfulness of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

Did you know? The three Jews had been appointed over the administration of the province of Babylon, but despite their public positions, they refused to serve the king’s gods or bow down to the golden statue.

Did you know? Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego declared that they did not need to defend themselves before the king: their God could save them, but even if he did not, they would not serve Nebuchadnezzar’s gods or bow down to the statue.

Did you know? After the three men answered him, Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury and ordered the furnace to be heated seven times hotter than usual; the soldiers who threw them into the furnace were killed by the flames.

Did you know? Nebuchadnezzar saw four men walking unharmed inside the furnace, even though the three Jews had been thrown into it bound. He described the fourth figure as resembling a “son of the gods.”
Did you know? After they came out of the furnace, it was clear that the fire had not harmed their bodies, singed their hair, or damaged their clothes; not even the smell of fire clung to them.
